questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using Multiple Instances of the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $h$ as the composite function

$$
h={5}^{u},\,u=\operatorname{ln}⁡v\,v=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}u}={5}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡5,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}=\frac{1}{v},\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\cdot \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={5}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\cdot (\frac{1}{v})\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-{5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we compute ${h}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(0) & =-{5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡0)}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\operatorname{tan}⁡0 \\  & =-{5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡1}\operatorname{ln}⁡5(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using Multiple Instances of the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\sqrt{u},\,u=\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,v=2x-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\cdot \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-1)}}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-1))\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-1)}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-1)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-1)}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f$ as the composite function

$$
f={u}^{4},\,u=\operatorname{cot}⁡v,\,v=5x-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=4{u}^{3},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}=-{csc}^{2}⁡v,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\cdot \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} \\  & =4{u}^{3}\cdot (-{csc}^{2}⁡v)\cdot 5 \\  & =4(\operatorname{cot}⁡(5x-1))^{3}\cdot (-{csc}^{2}⁡(5x-1))\cdot 5 \\  & =-20{cot}^{3}⁡(5x-1){csc}^{2}⁡(5x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now we compute ${f}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =-20{cot}^{3}⁡(5(0)-1){csc}^{2}⁡(5(0)-1) \\  & =-20{cot}^{3}⁡(-1){csc}^{2}⁡(-1) \\  & =-20(-{cot}^{3}⁡1){csc}^{2}⁡1 \\  & =20{cot}^{3}⁡1{csc}^{2}⁡1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u={v}^{2},\,v=x+6.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-{csc}^{2}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}=2v,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1.
$$

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\cdot \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-{csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot (2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2(x+6){csc}^{2}⁡[(x+6)^{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules
questions.worked_solution:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x+2).$ Then

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2x,\,{v}^{′}(x)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+2).
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(2x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x+2))+({x}^{2})(5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+2)) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x+2)+5{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.$ Then

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,\,{v}^{′}(x)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u$ and $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)(\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3x) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})|}_{x=\pi /2} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)=x+1$ and $v(x)={e}^{9x}.$ Then

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=1,\,{v}^{′}(x)=9{e}^{9x}.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(1)({e}^{9x})+(x+1)(9{e}^{9x}) \\  & ={e}^{9x}+9(x+1){e}^{9x} \\  & =(1+9(x+1)){e}^{9x} \\  & =(9x+10){e}^{9x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules
questions.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)={e}^{3x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x+2.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=3{e}^{3x},\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3{e}^{3x})(x+2)-{e}^{3x}(1)}{(x+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3x+6-1)\,{e}^{3x}}{(x+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3x+5)\,{e}^{3x}}{(x+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of ${y}^{′}(x)$ at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =\frac{(3(1)+5)({e}^{3(1)})}{((1)+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{8{e}^{3}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules
questions.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=3{x}^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)=(3x+5)^{2}.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=6x,\,{v}^{′}(x)=6(3x+5).
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(6x){(3x+5)}^{2}-(3{x}^{2})\cdot 6(3x+5)}{{((3x+5)^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6x(3x+5)(3x+5-3x)}{{(3x+5)}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6x(3x+5)(5)}{{(3x+5)}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{30x}{{(3x+5)}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules
questions.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)$ and the denominator $v(x)=x.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))(x)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(1)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{-3(\frac{\pi }{2})sin\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})-cos\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})}{{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3(\frac{\pi }{2})(-1)-0}{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules
questions.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=(x+1)^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)={x}^{2}+1.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2(x+1),\,{v}^{′}(x)=2x.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2(x+1))({x}^{2}+1)-((x+1)^{2})(2x)}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)({x}^{2}+1)-2x(x+1)^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)(({x}^{2}+1)-x(x+1))}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)({x}^{2}+1-{x}^{2}-x)}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)(1-x)}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(1-{x}^{2})}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2)$ and the denominator $v(x)=4x.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=7{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2),\,{v}^{′}(x)=4.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(7{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2))(4x)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2)(4)}{(4x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4(7x{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2))}{16{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{⧸}4(7x{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2))}{\text{⧸}4(4{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{7x{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2)}{4{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using Multiple Instances of the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as a composite function

$$
y = u^4, \qquad u = \cos{v}, \qquad v = 2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 4u^3,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d v} = -\sin{v},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm d x} = 2.
$$

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\cdot \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} \\  & =4{u}^{3}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot (2) \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{3}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\cdot (2) \\  & =-8{cos}^{3}⁡2x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x) = e^{-2x}$ and $v(x)=\tan{(x^2)}.$ Then

$$
u'(x) = -2e^{-2x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2x\sec^2(x^2).
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate both $u$ and $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(-2{e}^{-2x})\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})+{e}^{-2x}\cdot 2x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2}) \\  & =2{e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})+x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})) \\  & =2{e}^{-2x}(x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})-\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=e^{3x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=2^x +1.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x) = 3e^{3x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2^x \ln 2.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}	&= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \[5pt]
			        			&=\dfrac{3e^{3x} \cdot  \left( 2^{x}+1\right) - e^{3x} \cdot \left(2^x \cdot \ln2\right)}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\[5pt]
							&=\dfrac{3e^{3x}2^{x} + 3e^{3x} - e^{3x}2^{x}\ln 2}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\[5pt]
							&=\dfrac{e^{3x}  \left( 3(2^{x}) - 2^{x} \ln 2 +3\right)}{\left(2^{x}+1 \right)^2}
		}
$$
